summary: Defines EAP-PAX, a lightweight Extensible Authentication Protocol method that proves identity using a shared secret key. It can also support key provisioning, key management, identity protection and authenticated data exchange. This memo is informational.

eli5.summary: Two friends each know a secret handshake. EAP-PAX lets them prove they know it without saying the secret out loud, and then agree on a new private code for talking.

subtitle: Lightweight authentication using a shared secret with optional key provisioning and identity protection.

tldr.problem: Wireless networks need a simple, lightweight authentication method that can prove a device knows a shared secret without transmitting it, and support secure key updates when the initial key is weak.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-PAX defines two subprotocols: PAX_STD uses symmetric cryptography for basic mutual authentication, while PAX_SEC adds a server-side public key for identity protection and key provisioning with dictionary attack resistance.
tldr.outcome: EAP-PAX is informational and provides an alternative EAP authentication method. It was not widely adopted, and devices typically use other EAP methods like EAP-TLS or EAP-MSCHAPv2 instead.

today: RFC 4746 is an Informational document and has not been updated or obsoleted. However, EAP-PAX was never widely deployed in practice. Today, wireless networks typically use other EAP methods such as EAP-TLS (with certificates), EAP-MSCHAPv2 (Microsoft's variant), or EAP-PEAP (Protected EAP). These alternatives achieved greater industry support and deployment.

sections.title: Introduction to EAP-PAX
sections.content: EAP-PAX (Password Authenticated eXchange) is a lightweight authentication method for the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), designed especially for wireless networks. It authenticates devices using a shared secret key that both the client and server know. The protocol supports optional features including key provisioning (generating strong keys from weak passwords), key updates, identity protection, and authenticated data exchange. EAP-PAX is designed to work with weak initial keys like PINs, and uses a Diffie-Hellman key exchange to provide forward secrecy during updates.
sections.eli5: EAP-PAX is a way for a device and a server to prove they know the same secret without telling anyone what it is, and to create new secret codes that stay safe even if someone learns the old secret.

sections.title: Two Protocols: STD and SEC
sections.content: EAP-PAX defines two separate subprotocols. PAX_STD is the lightweight version, using only symmetric cryptography (keyed hashing). It authenticates the client and server to each other using shared keys, with optional authenticated data exchange. PAX_SEC is a more secure variant that requires an EAP server to have a public key (either a raw key or a certificate signed by a trusted Certificate Authority). PAX_SEC protects user identities from being revealed and prevents offline dictionary attacks when provisioning weak initial keys. The choice between PAX_STD and PAX_SEC depends on the security policy and deployment scenario.
sections.eli5: There are two modes: a simple one that just uses shared secrets, and a fancy one that also uses the server's public key to hide the user's name and protect weak passwords.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Session Keys
sections.content: EAP-PAX generates a series of keys from a master key derived during authentication. When a key update is being performed, the client and server exchange Diffie-Hellman exponents instead of raw random values, providing forward secrecy. From the shared entropy, the protocol derives multiple keys: a Master Key (MK) for session keys, a Confirmation Key (CK) to prove knowledge of the authentication key, an Integrity Check Key (ICK) to protect packet integrity, and finally Master Session Keys (MSK) and Extended Master Session Keys (EMSK) for export to other systems. The key derivation uses a specialized function called PAX-KDF that works with both 16-octet and 64-octet outputs depending on the key type.
sections.eli5: After proving they know the secret, the client and server make several different keys from it: some for checking that messages are real, some for creating new passwords, and some for talking securely.

sections.title: Packet Format and Protocol Flow
sections.content: EAP-PAX messages are organized around a fixed header containing an operation code (Op-Code), flags, and identifiers for the MAC algorithm, Diffie-Hellman group, and public key encryption method used. The payload follows a length-value encoding format. PAX_STD uses 4 message exchanges (PAX_STD-1 through PAX_STD-3 plus an optional PAX-ACK), while PAX_SEC uses 6 exchanges (PAX_SEC-1 through PAX_SEC-5 plus PAX-ACK). The operation code values identify which message is being sent: codes 0x01-0x03 are for PAX_STD, codes 0x11-0x15 are for PAX_SEC, and 0x21 is the acknowledgment. All messages are integrity-protected using an Integrity Check Value (ICV) computed over the entire packet.
sections.eli5: EAP-PAX messages have a fixed structure with a label saying what kind of message it is, and a payload with the actual data. Each message is protected with a checksum so nobody can change it.

sections.title: Security Properties and Threats
sections.content: EAP-PAX is designed to resist several threats. Both PAX_STD and PAX_SEC provide mutual authentication and replay protection. PAX_STD uses purely symmetric operations, making it fast but offering less protection for weak initial keys. PAX_SEC requires server-side public key operations to provide identity protection and resist offline dictionary attacks when provisioning, but the strength depends on the certificate mode chosen. In the weakest mode (raw public keys), the protocol is vulnerable to an offline dictionary attack during provisioning. In strict mode (CA-signed certificates), it is provably secure under the Random Oracle model. The protocol supports negotiation of ciphersuites and provides a minimum of 128 bits of key strength through the use of 256-bit Diffie-Hellman exponents and HMAC-SHA1 or HMAC-SHA256 hashing.
sections.eli5: EAP-PAX can check that both sides are who they claim to be, and protects against replaying old messages. If the server uses a certificate signed by a trusted company, it's very secure. If the server only uses its own keys, it's less secure when the password is weak.
